headline: Indonesia Halts Massive Deforestation Project, Saving 4 Million Acres
meta_description: Indonesia has paused its largest deforestation initiative after achieving rice self-sufficiency three years early, sparing 4 million acres of rainforest and pe…
summary_short: Indonesia has halted what was called the world's largest deforestation project after reaching its rice self-sufficiency goal ahead of schedule, protecting millions of ac…
body:
Indonesia's government has paused—and may have permanently halted—an enormous agricultural expansion that threatened some of the planet's most biodiverse landscapes. After achieving national rice self-sufficiency three years ahead of its original timeline, Indonesian authorities decided to spare approximately 4 million acres of rainforest, swamps, and peatlands from conversion to plantations. The decision came from an agreement between the agriculture and forestry ministries and the National Economic Council that future agricultural projects would use only land already in productive use, leaving pristine forest untouched.

The original plan had targeted vast tracts across Indonesian islands, particularly in Kalimantan and South Papua on the island of New Guinea, where carbon-rich peatlands were slated for conversion. Yet rapid progress in crop varieties, government fertilizer subsidies, and improved farming incentives meant the nation reached its self-sufficiency goal faster than expected. Hashim Djojohadikusumo, the president's younger brother and special envoy for climate and energy, announced in October that 4.4 million acres would remain untouched. "The government sees no further need to expand rice cultivation in so-called forest areas," he stated on behalf of the Agriculture Ministry.

The reversal marks a significant victory for environmental groups and indigenous communities who fiercely opposed the project. To date, about 90,000 acres had been converted to plantations. Going forward, according to officials Mari Elka Pangestu and the agriculture and forestry ministers, any expansion of subsidized agriculture—whether for food or bioethanol—will occur on the nation's existing 28 million acres of degraded land. Glenn Hurowitz, CEO of the monitoring organization Mighty Earth, called it "a globally significant decision for people, nature and climate," though he emphasized the need for ongoing monitoring and restoration work in affected areas.
quick_facts: 4 million acres of Indonesian rainforest spared from deforestation
Rice self-sufficiency achieved three years ahead of schedule
Peatlands in South Papua on New Guinea island protected
About 90,000 acres had already been converted before halt
Future agriculture to use 28 million acres of degraded land
